primitives.name: Unitary Utility Equivalence
primitives.verbatim_quote: The utility of any one unit is, in its effect on conduct, which is the only relevant consideration, exactly like that of any other; the essential fact is that as there are more units relatively, the utility per unit or·utility of any unit is relatively less.
primitives.latex: \frac{dU}{dN} < 0 \quad \text{where } U \text{ is total utility, } N \text{ is number of units}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'U(N)': 'total utility function of N units', 'dU/dN': 'marginal utility per unit'}
primitives.assumptions: Marginal utility decreases with quantity; individual units have equal impact on behavior.
primitives.breakdown_regime: At saturation point where additional units yield negligible utility gain.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that utility is not additive but relational—conflicts arise from shared, finite means of satisfaction. This leads to a dual structure: immediate wants and their wave-like alternation suggest temporal utility fluctuations, while the equivalence of units implies a uniform marginal contribution. These primitives form a kernel of decision-making under uncertainty, where agents navigate between conflicting satisfiers and oscillating desires. The failure mode occurs when static models assume constant utility or ignore intertemporal conflict. The mathematical framework must encode both the relational nature of utility and its temporal dynamics, using differential equations to model marginal utility decline and stochastic processes for want oscillations. This dualism underpins rational choice theory's limitations in capturing behavioral complexity.
